name: Hofkirche Innsbruck
kurzbeschreibung: The Hofkirche Innsbruck houses Emperor Maximilian I's sumptuous tomb flanked by 28 larger-than-life 'Schwarze Mander' and the 1558 Ebert organ.
preis: Erwachsene 9,00 €, Ermäßigte 7,00 €, unter 19 Jahren frei (Innsbruck Card inkludiert)
beschreibung:
Overview

The Hofkirche in Innsbruck – affectionately known locally as the Schwarzmander-Kirche – is Tyrol's preeminent sacred architectural monument and a burial place of European standing. Situated in the historic old town directly beside the Kaiserliche Hofburg, the three-aisled hall church was purpose-built in the 16th century to accommodate the monumental tomb monument for Emperor Maximilian I. The 28 larger-than-life bronze statues flanking the imperial cenotaph represent the pinnacle of Renaissance bronze-casting art in the entire German-speaking world.

History & Art Treasures

Emperor Maximilian I ("the Last Knight") had planned a monumental tomb before his death in 1519; however, in accordance with his wishes, he was laid to rest in his birthplace of Wiener Neustadt. His grandson, Emperor Ferdinand I., had the Hofkirche erected between 1553 and 1563 by master builder Andrea Crivelli to complete the emperor's legacy. The heart of the church is the empty ceremonial tomb (Kenotaph): a monumental sarcophagus crafted from black Adnet marble, adorned with 24 masterly white Carrara marble reliefs by sculptor Alexander Colin depicting Maximilian's deeds. Guarding the tomb are the legendary 28 Schwarzen Mander: larger-than-life bronze figures representing the emperor's real and mythical ancestors as well as contemporaries (including King Arthur of England, Theodoric the Great, Rudolf of Habsburg, and eight famous female rulers such as Mary of Burgundy and Bianca Maria Sforza). The statues were cast after designs by Albrecht Dürer and Jörg Kölderer by foundry masters such as Peter Vischer der Ältere and Gregor Löffler. Further priceless treasures include the Jörg-Ebert-Orgel from 1558 – one of the world's five most famous and oldest playable Renaissance organs –, the Silberne Kapelle containing the tomb of Archduke Ferdinand II and his bourgeois wife Philippine Welser, and the marble tomb of Tyrolean freedom hero Andreas Hofer, whose remains were transferred here in 1823.

Visit & Getting There

The Hofkirche forms part of the Tiroler Landesmuseen and is open Monday to Saturday from 09:00 to 17:00, and Sundays and public holidays from 12:30 to 17:00. Admission prices (as of the 2025/2026 season): regular adult €9.00, seniors and students €7.00, children and youths under 19 free; admission is free with the Innsbruck Card. Access is via the adjoining Volkskunstmuseum at Universitätsstraße 2. Getting there: only a few minutes' walk from Maria-Theresien-Straße and the Goldenes Dachl. Public transport: tram lines 1 and 3 or city buses to the Museumstraße or Congress stop. By car: underground car parks Citygarage or Congressgarage.

Tips

Via the entrance of the Volkskunstmuseum, the interior of the Hofkirche is barrier-free and accessible via lifts and ramps for wheelchairs and strollers (the Silberne Kapelle on the upper floor is accessible via a stairlift). Begin your tour with the multimedia presentation in the cloister, which vividly illustrates the life of Maximilian I.
